subtype: Village child in a city school [Receiver]
passage: On his first Monday at the city school in Ludhiana, Gurpreet, nine, walked in wearing his village sandals while everyone else wore black shoes. Someone giggled at the way he stretched his words. Gurpreet went quiet and kept his hands under the desk. Harish Sir, the class teacher, noticed in the second period. He didn't call attention to it. He said, "Gurpreet, would you tell us the word for a plough in your village? I'd like the class to learn it." Gurpreet whispered it. Harish Sir wrote it on the board. At lunch a boy named Manav shifted along the bench. "Sit here." By Friday Gurpreet was showing Manav how to make a paper kite the village way.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet wear on his first Monday?
qa.a: Gurpreet wore his village sandals while everyone else wore black shoes.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel when someone giggled at the way he spoke?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt ashamed and self-conscious. He went quiet and kept his hands under the desk.

qa.q: Which choice by Harish Sir turned shame toward confidence?
qa.a: Harish Sir asked Gurpreet to teach the class the village word for a plough and wrote it on the board, treating his knowledge as valuable.

qa.q: How might Manav have seen Gurpreet?
qa.a: As a new classmate worth making room for. Manav shifted along the bench and later learned how to make a paper kite from Gurpreet.

grounding: A child moving from a village to a city school feels behind, and a patient teacher and a friend to sit with turn shame into confidence.

"Sneha already said she would." "Then you already have a friend."

subtype: Village child in a city school [Receiver]
passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4, first week of July.
Suraj, nine, joined us from a village school near Sitapur. On his first day he sat alone at the back. When I asked him to read, he spoke Awadhi, and a few children laughed. He did not raise his hand again all week.
On Wednesday, Binita, one of the quieter girls, noticed he had no pencil box and shared hers. At lunch she showed him how the water tap worked.
I told the class calmly that Suraj knows every bird near his village. I asked him to draw one. He drew a kingfisher, perfectly.
Next step: I've seated Suraj with Binita and will give him ten minutes of reading practice daily.

qa.q: What bird did Suraj draw?
qa.a: He drew a kingfisher, perfectly.

qa.q: What does Suraj not raising his hand all week suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt ashamed and behind after the children laughed at his reading in Awadhi.

qa.q: What did the teacher and Binita do that could turn Suraj's shame into confidence?
qa.a: Binita shared her pencil box and showed him the tap, while the teacher praised his bird knowledge, seated him with a friend and planned daily reading practice.

qa.q: How might Binita feel helping Suraj?
qa.a: Binita may feel kind and proud, glad to be the friend he can sit with.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a village child feeling behind in a town school, and how encouragement, patient teaching and a friend help build confidence.

subtype: Village child in a city school [Receiver]
passage:
Dear Diary,
Second week at the school in Dehradun. Everyone here has shiny black shoes. Mine are the old brown ones from our village near Leh. Today a boy asked if I'd walked here on a yak. Everyone laughed. I laughed too so they wouldn't see my face.
I also didn't know what "canteen coupon" meant, so I didn't eat.
But then Ankita, who sits next to me, gave me half her paratha. She showed me how the coupons work. She said, "My Nani's village doesn't even have a road. You're not behind. You just came from far."
Ma'am asked me to tell the class about apricot season. I told them how we dry apricots on the roof. They asked so many questions!
Maybe tomorrow I'll be less scared.
Tenzin

qa.q: What did Ankita give Tenzin?
qa.a: Ankita gave Tenzin half her paratha.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin laugh along with the others?
qa.a: Tenzin felt embarrassed and hurt, and laughed so they wouldn't see the shame on Tenzin's face.

qa.q: What helped turn Tenzin's day around?
qa.a: Ankita shared food and explained the coupons kindly, and the teacher invited Tenzin to talk about apricot season, which made the class curious.

qa.q: How might Ankita see Tenzin's situation?
qa.a: Ankita sees Tenzin as not behind but simply from far away, thinking of her own Nani's village without a road.

grounding: A child from a village feels behind in a town school because of clothes and new words, and a friend and teacher help shame turn toward confidence.

subtype: Village child in a city school [Receiver]
passage:
When Chandrika, eight, moved from her village to the school in the kasba, she noticed everything: the girls had ribbons, said "sorry" in English, and knew the tables by heart.
On the second day, she whispered her answer and nobody heard. On the third, she didn't come out at break.
Ganga Didi, the teacher who ran the small library, found her inside. "Why aren't you playing?"
"I don't know anything here."
"You know how to milk a buffalo?"
"Yes."
"Then you know something none of them do." Ganga Didi pulled out a picture book. "Read one page to me each break. I'll help."
By the end of the month, Chandrika was reading the page aloud to two other girls, who sat on either side of her.

qa.q: Where did Ganga Didi find Chandrika?
qa.a: Ganga Didi found her inside the small library.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she said, "I don't know anything here"?
qa.a: Chandrika felt ashamed and behind, overwhelmed by all the ways the town girls seemed different.

qa.q: What did Ganga Didi do that built Chandrika's confidence?
qa.a: She reminded Chandrika of what she did know and offered patient daily reading help.

qa.q: How might the two girls see Chandrika by the end of the month?
qa.a: They likely see her as a friend and a good reader, not as the new girl from the village.

grounding: A village child in a small-town school feels behind, and a teacher's encouragement and patient teaching help turn shame into confidence.

subtype: Village child in a city school [Receiver]
passage: Aiko's first week at the big school in Osaka felt like running after a train. In her mountain village there had been eleven children in one classroom; here there were thirty-four, and they all seemed to know where the shoe lockers were without looking. Her words came out slow and countryish, and when she used her village word for "I", two boys snorted. At lunch she ate facing the wall. On Thursday Mr. Tanaka, the class teacher, asked Javier to show her the recycling rules, which had five different bins. Javier had moved from Valencia only last year. "I put glass in paper for a month," he told her. "Everyone laughs at first. Then they forget." On Friday Mr. Tanaka asked Aiko to tell the class how to plant rice. She knew every step.

qa.q: How many children were in Aiko's village classroom?
qa.a: There were eleven children in one classroom.

qa.q: What was Aiko feeling when she ate lunch facing the wall?
qa.a: Aiko felt embarrassed and behind, wanting to hide after the boys snorted at her village word.

qa.q: How did Mr. Tanaka help Aiko move from shame toward confidence?
qa.a: He paired her with a friendly classmate for the new rules and then let her teach something she knew well, planting rice.

qa.q: Why might Javier understand Aiko better than the other children?
qa.a: Javier had also moved recently and made mistakes like putting glass in paper, so he knows how embarrassing the first weeks feel and that it passes.

grounding: It illustrates a village child in a city school who feels behind, and how patient teaching and a classmate to sit with begin to turn shame into confidence.
